summary: Describes LDIF, a text file format for describing directory entries or changes to them. It is widely used to import, export and modify LDAP directory data. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: LDIF is a text file for directory information, the records an LDAP server keeps about people and devices. It can hold whole entries, or it can hold a list of changes to make. Because it is plain text, a short script can produce one from any database.

questions: how to fold lines in ldif
subtitle: A plain-text file format for moving directory entries in and out of an LDAP server, and for describing changes to them.

tldr.problem: Directory data has to move between servers and out of legacy systems, and a common interchange format makes that practical. The format also has to express changes, not just whole entries.
tldr.mechanism: LDIF is a sequence of records separated by line separators. Each record either lists the attributes of one directory entry, or describes one change to an entry, with the change types add, delete, modify and modrdn matching the LDAP operations one to one.
tldr.outcome: A file can be imported into any LDAP server regardless of its internal database representation, and the RFC requires UTF-8 data, base64 encoding for unsafe characters, and defines line folding and comment rules. It warns that LDIF carries no authentication and can pull in external files.

facts.label: Change record types
facts.value: add, delete, modify, modrdn or moddn

facts.label: End of a modification
facts.value: A line holding a single hyphen

today: RFC 2849 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2000. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Common File Format
sections.content:
There are a number of situations where a common interchange format is desirable. One might wish to export a copy of the contents of a directory server to a file, move that file to a different machine, and import the contents into a second directory server.

By using a well-defined interchange format, the development of data import tools from legacy systems is facilitated. A fairly simple set of tools written in awk or perl can convert a database of personnel information into an LDIF file, and that file can then be imported into a directory server regardless of the internal database representation the target server uses.

The LDIF format was originally developed and used in the University of Michigan LDAP implementation, where the first use was to describe directory entries. Later the format was expanded to allow the representation of changes to directory entries. The RFC also relates LDIF to the application/directory MIME content-type of RFC 2425, a general framework for conveying directory information that is independent of any particular directory service. LDIF is a simpler format which is perhaps easier to create, and it may also be used to describe a set of changes to be applied to a directory.
sections.plainLanguage: Two directories rarely store data the same way inside. A common text file format lets you take data out of one and put it into another, and lets a small script convert an old database into that file.

sections.title: What an LDIF File Contains
sections.content:
The LDIF format is used to convey directory information, or a description of a set of changes made to directory entries. An LDIF file consists of a series of records separated by line separators. A record consists of a sequence of lines describing a directory entry, or a sequence of lines describing a set of changes to a directory entry. An LDIF file specifies a set of directory entries, or a set of changes to be applied to directory entries, but not both.

There is a one-to-one correlation between the LDAP operations that modify the directory, which are add, delete, modify and modrdn, and the types of change record described in the syntax. This correspondence is intentional, and it permits a straightforward translation from LDIF change records to protocol operations.
sections.plainLanguage: A file holds either whole entries or a list of changes, never both. Each kind of change matches one LDAP operation, so a file can be applied to a server without translation.

sections.title: The Formal Syntax
sections.content:
The definition uses the augmented Backus-Naur Form specified in RFC 2234. A file is ldif-content or ldif-changes, and both start with a version specification and then a series of records. A content record is a distinguished name followed by attribute value specifications; a change record is a distinguished name, optional controls, and a change record.

The version number MUST be 1 for the format described here. A distinguished name is written after dn:, either as a plain string or base64 encoded after a second colon. An attribute value specification is an attribute description, which may carry options separated by semicolons, followed by a value specification. A value specification is a plain string after one colon, a base64 string after two colons, or a URL after :<.

The change record types are add, delete, modify and modrdn or moddn. A modify record contains one or more modification specifications, each of which is an add, delete or replace operation on one attribute, followed by its values, and terminated by a line containing a hyphen.
sections.plainLanguage: Each line starts with a label. A name and a value follow, and a second colon in front of a value means the value is base64 encoded. Change lines name the kind of change and the entry it applies to.

sections.title: Notes on Folding, Comments and Encoding
sections.content:
Any non-empty line, including comment lines, may be folded by inserting a line separator and a space. Folding MUST NOT occur before the first character of the line, so folding a line into two lines, the first of which is empty, is not permitted. A line that begins with a single space is a continuation of the previous non-empty line, and when folded lines are joined exactly one space at the beginning of each continued line must be discarded. Implementations SHOULD NOT fold lines in the middle of a multi-byte UTF-8 character. Any line that begins with a pound sign is a comment line and MUST be ignored when parsing.

Any distinguished name, relative distinguished name or value that contains characters outside the safe set, or begins with a character outside the safe starting set, MUST be base64 encoded; other values MAY be base64 encoded. A zero-length attribute value must be written as the attribute description, a colon, and a newline. Values or distinguished names that end with a space SHOULD be base64 encoded.

Distinguished names, relative distinguished names and attribute values of DirectoryString syntax must be valid UTF-8. Implementations that read LDIF may interpret files stored in another character set, but they MUST NOT generate LDIF content which does not contain valid UTF-8 data.

When a URL is given in an attribute value specification, implementations SHOULD support the file:// URL format, and the contents of the referenced file are to be included verbatim in the interpreted output. Implementations MAY support other URL formats.

When controls are included in an LDIF file, implementations MAY choose to ignore some or all of them. This may be necessary if the changes are being sent on an LDAPv2 connection, which does not support controls, or if the remote server does not support them. If the criticality of a control is true, the implementation MUST either include the control, or MUST NOT send the operation to a remote server.
sections.plainLanguage: Long values may be split over two lines, with the second line starting with a space. A line starting with a hash is a comment. Anything with awkward characters is written base64 encoded so it cannot break the file.

sections.title: The Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives seven examples. The first is a simple file with two entries, each starting with a distinguished name and then listing attributes such as objectclass, cn, sn, uid and telephonenumber.

The second shows a folded attribute value, where a long description is split across two lines with the continuation starting with a space. The third shows a base64 encoded value, written after two colons and continued over several lines. The fourth shows UTF-8 encoded values with language tags, such as ou;lang-ja::, and comments that state what the encoded values contain.

The fifth shows a reference to an external file, with the value written as jpegphoto:< file:///usr/local/directory/photos/hjensen.jpg. The sixth shows a series of change records with comments: an add, a delete, a modrdn that renames an entry, a modrdn that also moves an entry to a new location with a newsuperior line, and a modify record that adds, deletes and replaces attributes, each modification separated by a line holding a single hyphen. The seventh shows a change record with a control attached, using the Tree Delete Control with criticality true.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples cover the cases you meet in practice: whole entries, a value split over two lines, a value in base64, text in other languages, a link to a file on disk, and lists of changes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Given typical directory applications, an LDIF file is likely to contain sensitive personal data, so appropriate measures should be taken to protect the privacy of the people whose data it contains.

Because :< directives can cause external content to be included when processing an LDIF file, one should be cautious about accepting LDIF files from external sources. A trojan LDIF file could name a file with sensitive contents and cause it to be included in a directory entry, which a hostile entity could then read over LDAP.

LDIF does not provide any method for carrying authentication information with a file. Users of LDIF files must take care to verify the integrity of an LDIF file received from an external source.
sections.plainLanguage: These files hold personal details, so they need protecting. A file that pulls in the contents of another file can be used to read data that should stay private, and the format itself carries no way to prove who sent it.

items.label: Add
items.desc: Adds an entry with the attributes that follow.

items.label: Delete
items.desc: Deletes the entry named by the distinguished name.

items.label: Modify
items.desc: Adds, deletes or replaces values of attributes.

items.label: Rename
items.desc: Also written moddn. Renames the entry, and can move it with a newsuperior line.

viz.caption: THE THREE WAYS TO WRITE AN ATTRIBUTE VALUE

items.title: Plain value
items.text: One colon in front of the value.

items.title: Base64 value
items.text: Two colons in front of the encoded value.

items.title: URL reference
items.text: A colon and a less-than sign in front of the URL.

viz.caption: EXAMPLE 1: A SIMPLE LDIF FILE WITH TWO ENTRIES

data.title: An LDIF file
data.code:
version: 1
dn: cn=Barbara Jensen, ou=Product Development, dc=airius, dc=com
objectclass: top
objectclass: person
objectclass: organizationalPerson
cn: Barbara Jensen
cn: Barbara J Jensen
cn: Babs Jensen
sn: Jensen
uid: bjensen
telephonenumber: +1 408 555 1212
description: A big sailing fan.

dn: cn=Bjorn Jensen, ou=Accounting, dc=airius, dc=com
objectclass: top
objectclass: person
objectclass: organizationalPerson
cn: Bjorn Jensen
sn: Jensen
telephonenumber: +1 408 555 1212

viz.caption: EXAMPLE 6, EXCERPT: A MODIFY CHANGE RECORD

data.title: A modify change record
data.code:
dn: cn=Paula Jensen, ou=Product Development, dc=airius, dc=com
changetype: modify
add: postaladdress
postaladdress: 123 Anystreet $ Sunnyvale, CA $ 94086
-

delete: description
-

replace: telephonenumber
telephonenumber: +1 408 555 1234
telephonenumber: +1 408 555 5678
-
